rv.q: That’s what’s currently happening in the Lunt-Fontanne, and thanks to the swift, smart construction of Summer, which neither overburdens its material nor overstays its welcome, it’s a pretty damn good time.
Instead what you get here is what you usually get: a valedictory experience, not an honest story, only tolerable for die-hard fans.

Despite the exciting vocalism of a cast led by the formidable LaChanze, it reduces the late Queen of Disco and pioneer of electronica to a few factoids and song samples that make her seem profoundly inconsequential.
Though the show hits its marks with the reliability of a metronome, it never builds to the transcendence that Summer's music can provide.
What saves 'Summer' from complete mediocrity is the singing of LaChanze, Ariana DeBose and Storm Lever
But you won’t get much of a sense the times in "Summer: The Donna Summer Musical," a narrow-minded jukebox musical that views its titular heroine in a vacuum.

A jukebox musical that could undo all the genre rehab delivered by superior shows built around Carole King and, if you want to stretch the definition a bit to include Lazarus, David Bowie, Broadway‘s Summer: The Donna Summer Musical, opening tonight, is as unimaginative as its title.
Anyone who worked as hard for her money - and for a professional respect that came too late - as Donna Summer did deserves so much more than this.
Staged with ruthless efficiency by director Des McAnuff, who previously led one of Broadway's best-ever bio-musicals Jersey Boys to worldwide success.

Sadly, that’s one of the few decent jokes in this tacky little show, a feebly dramatized Wikipedia page with lackluster covers, which was rushed to Broadway following a fall tryout at La Jolla Playhouse that received mostly tepid reviews.
I thoroughly enjoyed myself and was very pleased to have seen it.
Summer: The Donna Summer Musical delivers the seasonal sunshine. It just doesn't also bring a whole lotta depth.
Nearly six years after her death, Donna Summer remains one of the most underappreciated singers of her time, in part because of the unfairly maligned genre she was associated with.

The performances are frequently electric, and the songs sound spectacular, but any attempt to learn something about Summer's life comes and goes as quickly and lightly as that barely acknowledged tumor.
Enough is enough with Broadway jukebox musicals stitched together with threadbare and synthetic stories.

cn.t: Critics find this jukebox musical disappointingly generic despite Donna Summer's iconic catalog, though the show delivers with powerhouse vocal performances from its three leads and infectious dance hits that still get audiences moving.

sg.ra: Per SeatPlan and Headout, center rows D-J are the Lunt-Fontanne sweet spot because the house stage sits unusually high and is not raked — patrons halfway back in orchestra report they cannot see the stage floor, so anchoring forward of the overhang line (row W) but back from rows A-C keeps the stage floor visible.

Front Mezz is only 5 rows deep (A-E) with no balcony above, so every row has clean sightlines — and row B specifically beats row A because a safety railing in front of row A cuts into the stage (one source cites ~35% obstruction for some seats), making B the preferred pick that most guides name by row.

SeatPlan and forum posts flag that the mezzanine overhang starts at row J but begins cutting into the top of the stage from row W back across Left, Center, and Right Orchestra — combined with the Lunt-Fontanne's high unraked stage (floor already hard to see from mid-orchestra), rear orchestra loses both the top and bottom of the picture.

The Lunt-Fontanne has no balcony, so unlike most large Nederlander houses the Rear Mezz has zero overhang — SeatPlan specifically names rows B-C as best because they clear the railing behind the Front Mezz that can obstruct row A, and the section's rake keeps sightlines clean despite being the cheapest seats in the venue.

Multiple guides flag that the Lunt-Fontanne's unusually high, non-raked stage makes rows A-C worse than typical Broadway front rows — Headout and TickPick-linked guides warn sightlines can be obstructed because the stage is raised, and any tall patron in front blocks center-stage action at this proximity.
